Chapter 4: Dehumanization and the Loss of Empathy
When we start seeing people as less than human, something unsettling happens.
It becomes way too easy to treat them badly. This process, called dehumanization, doesn’t usually shout its arrival.
Most of the time, it slips in quietly—through the words we use, the labels we slap on others, or even the uniforms they wear. Little by little, these things chip away at our empathy, making it easier to justify actions that, not long ago, would’ve felt unthinkable.
Picture a schoolyard. There’s a group of kids, and they start calling one classmate a cruel nickname.
At first, it feels like a joke. But the name sticks. Suddenly, that student turns into “the outsider”—someone it’s okay to ignore or mock.
The rest of the group, caught up in the moment, stop seeing their classmate as a real person with feelings and dreams. The teasing ramps up, and what started as “just fun” turns into something truly harmful.
And you know what? This same pattern plays out on a much bigger scale.
In prisons, for example, people are called by numbers, not names. In some workplaces, employees get reduced to “resources” or “units.” In times of conflict, the enemy is painted as evil or less than human.
With every step, it becomes easier to ignore someone’s pain, and to justify harsh treatment.
But here’s something to pay attention to—the process is usually gradual.
Most of us don’t just wake up and decide to be cruel. Instead, we get used to small acts of distancing—using labels, following orders, going along with the crowd.
Over time, these habits wear down our empathy, making it possible to do things we never thought we would.
So, what’s the antidote?
It’s about remembering the humanity in others, even when everything around us pushes for distance.
That might mean using someone’s name instead of a number, listening instead of judging, or just pausing for a moment to imagine what someone else might be feeling.
Of course, it’s not always easy—especially when the pressure is on.
But if we stay connected to empathy, we can resist the pull of dehumanization, and act with kindness, even when it’s tough.
